definition: A failure in which a component simply stops working and sends nothing more. It is the easiest failure to handle, but over a network other machines can only suspect it, because a crashed node looks the same as a very slow one.
example: A kernel panic or an out-of-memory kill is a crash failure.

definition: A failure in which a component is running but some requests or replies are lost and never answered. To the caller it looks like a timeout.
example: A message broker that silently discards messages when its queue is full is producing omission failures.

definition: A failure in which a component gives correct answers but too late to be useful. Slow-but-alive components can be more damaging than dead ones because callers keep waiting on them.
example: A server that normally replies in 20 ms but now takes 8 seconds has a timing failure.

definition: A failure in which a component behaves arbitrarily: it may return wrong or inconsistent answers, through a bug, corrupted data or deliberate malice. It is the hardest failure model to tolerate.
example: A replica that reports a different account balance to each node it talks to is behaving in a Byzantine way.

definition: A network model with no upper bound on how long a message may take or how slowly a process may run. In such a network you cannot reliably tell a crashed node from a slow one.
OOM means out of memory. When a machine runs out of RAM, the operating system (on Linux, the OOM killer) terminates a process to free memory, which looks like a sudden crash.
example: An API whose in-memory queue grew to 40 GB was OOM-killed, losing everything in the queue.

definition: A fatal error in the operating system kernel from which it cannot safely recover, so the whole machine stops and usually reboots.
Designing a component to stop or return an error immediately when something is wrong, instead of waiting or continuing in a broken state. It keeps failures small, quick and visible.
example: A circuit breaker that is open fails fast: the caller gets an error in microseconds instead of waiting for a timeout.

definition: A request or message that reliably crashes or breaks whatever processes it. Retrying it or spreading it to other servers spreads the damage.
example: A malformed upload that crashes every image worker that tries to resize it is a poison request.

definition: A line around part of a system (a host, zone, region or cell) that a failure is designed not to cross. Choosing boundaries decides how big an outage can get.
The expected fraction of devices of a given type that fail within a year.
example: At a 2% annual failure rate, 10,000 disks lose about 200 a year.

definition: A dependency that must be working for a request to succeed. Availabilities of serial dependencies multiply, so the whole is less available than its weakest part.
example: A 99.9% service calling a 99.9% database has at most about 99.8% availability.

definition: Automatically copying data again from surviving replicas after a disk or node holding a copy fails, to restore the intended number of copies.
Google Cloud Platform, Google's public cloud computing services.

Google's free books on how it runs production systems, chiefly Site Reliability Engineering (2016) and The Site Reliability Workbook (2018). They are widely used as references for SLOs, alerting and overload handling.
AWS's published set of design principles and best practices for cloud workloads, organised into pillars such as reliability and security.
A written review after an incident that records what happened, its impact and causes, and the actions that will stop it recurring. In SRE practice it is blameless.
A failure that will happen again on every attempt, such as a malformed request or a permission error. Retrying it only wastes capacity.
The full spread of how long requests take, usually summarised by percentiles or stored as a histogram, rather than a single average.

Small probe packets TCP can send on an idle connection to check the other end is still there. With Linux's defaults the first probe is sent only after 2 hours of idleness, so a dead peer goes unnoticed for over two hours, and a slow but live server never trips it at all.

A queueing policy described by Facebook: serve requests first-in-first-out normally, but switch to newest-first when a queue builds up, because the newest requests' clients are the ones still waiting.
The rate of useful work completed: requests finished successfully while the client was still waiting. Under overload, throughput can stay high while goodput collapses.
A state where a system is fully busy but does almost no useful work, because it spends its capacity on requests that have already timed out and on retries.
The amount of work arriving at a system, whether or not it can handle it.

The three modes of a circuit breaker: closed (calls pass through and failures are counted), open (calls fail immediately without reaching the dependency) and half-open (after a cool-down, a few trial calls test whether the dependency has recovered).
A time window that moves forward continuously, such as "the last 10 seconds" or "the last 28 days", so old events drop out as new ones arrive.
A call that takes longer than a configured threshold. Counting slow calls as failures lets a circuit breaker react to gray failure, not just errors.
A Java library providing circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiters, retries and time limiters.
A .NET library for resilience patterns such as retry, circuit breaker and timeout.
A cap on how many requests a server or client processes at the same time; requests beyond it are rejected or queued.
example: A server doing 2,000 req/s at 40 ms with 25% margin might cap concurrency at 100.

definition: A priority label on a request saying how important it is. Google tags requests from most to least important as CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS and SHEDDABLE, and sheds the least important first.

Client-side load control described in the Google SRE book: each client tracks how many requests the backend recently accepted and drops some new requests itself once the backend is rejecting many, saving the backend the cost of rejecting them.
The gRPC status code meaning a resource such as a quota or capacity has run out; clients should back off.
Consumers fetch messages at their own pace instead of having them pushed. A slow consumer then falls behind (lag grows) rather than being overwhelmed.

An append-only record of messages written to disk and usually replicated, from which consumers read at their own pace. Kafka is the usual example. It survives crashes but still has finite capacity and retention.

A fallback that serves precomputed or cached data (for example a fixed bestseller list) instead of calling another live system when a dependency fails. AWS's Builders' Library prefers these, or a 'fallback' path used all the time, because rarely run fallback code is poorly tested and can overload whatever it falls back to.
example: If the recommendations service is down, the home page shows a bestseller list built overnight rather than querying a second recommendation engine.

definition: Malicious software that encrypts or steals an organisation's data and demands payment. Isolated, immutable backups are the main defence for recovery.
The SQL statement that deletes a whole table and its data. Replication copies it to replicas, so only backups can undo it.
The SQL statement that removes rows from a table. Without a WHERE clause it removes every row.
Data damage caused by valid but wrong operations, such as a buggy release, an accidental DELETE or an attacker, rather than by hardware. Replication faithfully copies it, so it needs backups.
Continuously copying a database's write-ahead log files to separate storage. Together with a base backup it allows point-in-time recovery; how often segments leave the server sets the achievable RPO.
A backup guideline: keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media or services, with 1 copy off-site.
A backup that cannot be changed or deleted until a retention period ends, even by administrators, so ransomware or a compromised account cannot destroy it.

The two retention modes of Amazon S3 Object Lock. In compliance mode no user, including the account's root user, can overwrite or delete a protected object version or shorten its retention until it expires. In governance mode users with the special s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can override the lock.
example: Backups locked in compliance mode for 30 days survive even an attacker who has stolen the AWS root credentials.

definition: Actually restoring a backup into a working system on a schedule to prove it works and measure how long it takes.
Re-applying the changes recorded in a transaction log to a restored backup, to bring it forward to a later point in time.
The cheapest disaster recovery strategy: keep backups in another region and, after a disaster, provision infrastructure and restore. RPO and RTO are typically hours.

A disaster recovery strategy that keeps the core data layer (such as a replicated database) running in the recovery region while application servers are off; in a disaster you scale them up. RPO is minutes and RTO tens of minutes.
Defining servers, networks and other infrastructure in version-controlled files that tools apply automatically, so environments can be rebuilt reliably.
A Netflix tool that randomly terminates production instances so teams must build services that survive it. Chaos Gorilla and Chaos Kong simulated losing a zone and a region.
Google's company-wide Disaster Recovery Testing exercises, in which teams deliberately break systems and processes to check recovery works.
Keeping software always releasable and shipping changes through an automated pipeline; continuous deployment goes further and releases every passing change automatically.
Giving every person, service or job only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them, so a compromise or bug does limited damage.
Collecting and watching predefined measurements of a system so you are told when something is wrong.
A timestamped record of a discrete event written by a program, such as a request, error or external call. Logs give detail for investigation.
A severity tag on a log record, such as debug, info, warn or error, used to filter and sample logs.
A key-value pair attached to a metric, such as route="/pay", that splits it into separate time series. Unbounded label values (like user IDs) explode the number of series.
A metric that only goes up (except for resetting to zero on restart), such as total requests served. You graph its rate of increase.
example: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) turns a request counter into requests per second.

definition: A metric that can go up and down and shows a current value, such as queue depth or memory in use.
One range in a histogram, holding the count of observations up to its upper edge. Percentiles inside a bucket are only estimates, so edges should sit at important thresholds.
Estimating a value inside a histogram bucket by assuming observations are spread evenly across it. The true value could be anywhere in the bucket.
Prometheus's query language. rate() turns a counter into a per-second rate; histogram_quantile() estimates a percentile from histogram buckets.
In Prometheus, periodically fetching the current metric values from each target over HTTP.
A Prometheus rule that precomputes a query on a schedule and saves the result as a new time series, so alerts and dashboards are cheap to evaluate.
A sample trace ID attached to a metric data point, letting you jump from a latency spike to an example trace that caused it.
Writing logs as machine-readable key-value records (usually JSON) instead of free text, so they can be filtered and grouped by any field.
A pattern language for matching text. Parsing free-text logs with regexes is fragile compared with structured fields.
Removing or masking sensitive values (passwords, tokens, card numbers) before data is logged or shared.
Deciding whether to keep a trace at the start of the request, before its outcome is known, and passing that decision along. Cheap, but it keeps rare errors only at the sampling rate.
Deciding whether to keep a trace after all its spans have arrived, so all errors and slow traces can be kept. It needs collectors that buffer spans in memory.
A sampling rule in which each span follows its parent's keep-or-drop decision, so a trace is kept or dropped as a whole.
A service that receives telemetry from applications, processes it (batching, sampling, redacting) and exports it to backends.
The OpenTelemetry component that sends telemetry onward to a backend or another collector. A load-balancing exporter routes all spans of one trace to the same collector.
The OpenTelemetry Protocol, the standard wire format for sending traces, metrics and logs between SDKs, collectors and backends.
Passing trace context (trace ID, span ID, sampling flag) from one service to the next in headers or message properties, so spans join into one trace.
Google's distributed tracing system, described in a 2010 paper, which inspired open-source tracers such as Zipkin and Jaeger.
An open-source distributed tracing system originally built at Twitter, based on Google's Dapper paper.
An open-source distributed tracing platform originally built at Uber and now a CNCF project.
A checklist by Tom Wilkie for monitoring each request-driven service: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests) and Duration (latency distribution).
A checklist by Brendan Gregg for each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, pools): Utilisation, Saturation (queued work it can't yet serve) and Errors.
The amount of extra work a resource has that it can't service yet, usually waiting in a queue. It is the S in the USE method.
example: A CPU run queue of 20 threads on 8 cores shows saturation.

definition: The Google SRE book's four key measurements for a user-facing system: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
The list of threads ready to run but waiting for a CPU. A long run queue means the CPU is saturated.
When so many alerts fire, mostly needing no action, that on-call engineers start ignoring them and miss real problems.
Paging on what users experience (errors, latency, SLO burn) rather than on internal causes like high CPU, which may not matter. Cause metrics stay on dashboards for diagnosis.

A pre-agreed set of rules for what happens as the error budget is spent, for example freezing feature releases once it is exhausted and requiring a postmortem for any incident that uses more than 20% of it.

How fast a service is using its error budget, relative to the rate that would use it up exactly at the end of the window: the observed error rate divided by the budget rate. A burn rate of 2 empties the budget in half the window.
example: With a 0.1% budget, a 1.44% error rate is a burn rate of 14.4.

definition: The SRE workbook's recommended way of alerting on SLOs: several rules, each firing when the burn rate over both a long window and a short window exceeds a threshold, such as 14.4× over 1 hour and 5 minutes.
The period over which an alert rule averages its measurement. Long windows show a problem is significant; short windows show it is still happening, so the alert stops soon after a fix.
How long after a problem starts an alert fires.
A sequence of steps a user takes to achieve something important, such as search, add to basket and checkout. SLIs focus on these.
Sending artificial requests that imitate users, on a schedule, to check a service works end to end even when real traffic is low.
A bug of the highest priority (priority zero), needing immediate action. Error budget policies usually let P0 fixes ship even during a release freeze.
A period during which no new features or non-urgent changes are deployed, used for example when the error budget is exhausted.
An alert that opens a ticket for working hours instead of paging someone immediately, used for slow problems that are real but not urgent.
Treating shipping code to production (deploy) and turning its behaviour on for users (release) as separate steps, usually via feature flags, so a bad release can be undone without a deploy.
In a canary or experiment, the group running the old version at the same time and similar size, against which the new version's metrics are compared.
Software that statistically compares a canary's metrics with a baseline and decides automatically whether to continue or roll back. Kayenta (Spinnaker) and Argo Rollouts do this.
An open-source continuous delivery platform, originally from Netflix, used to run staged and canary deployments.
A Kubernetes controller that adds canary and blue-green deployment strategies with automated analysis.
Confidence that an observed difference (such as a higher canary error rate) is unlikely to be just random noise. It needs enough events.
How long a new version runs at a deployment stage, under watch, before the rollout moves on. It must be long enough for slow problems like memory leaks to show.
Deploying a change to a single host first, as the smallest possible stage of a rollout.
One step of a staged global rollout, such as one zone, one region, then larger groups of regions.
A short-lived feature flag that hides unfinished or newly deployed code until it is released, then is removed.
A feature flag that sends different users down different code paths for an A/B test.
A feature flag operators use to control system behaviour, such as a kill switch that disables an expensive feature under load.
A long-lived feature flag that enables features for particular users, such as premium or internal users.
A practice where developers merge small changes into the main branch frequently, hiding unfinished work behind feature flags instead of long-lived branches.
Deploying new code to production with its behaviour switched off, so it is present but not visible to users.
Responding to a bad release by shipping a new fix rather than rolling back. Usually slower and riskier under pressure.
Changing a data format safely in two deploys: first a version that can read both formats but still writes the old one, then a version that writes the new one. Rolling back the second step stays safe.
Changing an interface or schema in compatible steps: add the new form alongside the old (expand), migrate users and data, then remove the old form (contract).
A database column allowed to contain NULL (no value). Adding one is usually quick because existing rows need no data.
The SQL statement that changes a table's structure, such as adding or renaming a column. Some forms need an exclusive lock or rewrite the table.
The line of transactions waiting for a lock. In PostgreSQL a waiting ALTER TABLE blocks later queries behind it, so one stuck migration can stall a whole table.
A PostgreSQL setting that makes a statement give up if it waits longer than the given time for a lock, so a migration fails fast instead of stalling the table.
A schema change that makes the database copy every row into a new physical table, which can hold heavy locks for a long time on large tables.
Tools such as gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change that change a large MySQL table by copying it to a new table in the background and swapping it in, avoiding long locks.
The packaged output of a build (such as a container image or binary). Safe pipelines build it once and promote the same artefact through every stage.
The automated sequence that builds, tests and deploys software through stages to production.
Secure Shell: an encrypted protocol for logging in to and running commands on remote machines.
Stopping all old instances and then starting the new ones, which causes downtime in between.
A change to settings rather than code. It alters production behaviour just as a deploy does, so it should be staged and monitored the same way.
An urgent fix applied quickly to production, often skipping the usual process.
Short forms for authentication (proving who you are) and authorisation (deciding what you may do).
Encrypting stored data (disks, databases, backups) so it is unreadable without the key, protecting against stolen media or leaked copies but not against anyone who can query through the application.
Encrypting data while it travels over a network, usually with TLS.
Encrypting individual sensitive fields (such as card numbers) in the application with keys the database never sees, so database access alone does not reveal them.
Generating, storing, controlling access to, rotating and destroying cryptographic keys. Encryption is only as strong as the protection of its keys.
Hardware security module: tamper-resistant hardware that stores keys and performs cryptographic operations so the keys never leave it in plaintext.
Microsoft Azure's service for storing keys, secrets and certificates.
Encrypting data with a data key (DEK) locally, then encrypting that data key with a master key held in a KMS, and storing the encrypted DEK beside the data. Bulk data never goes to the KMS.
Data encryption key: the key that actually encrypts data, typically a 256-bit AES key. In envelope encryption it is stored only in encrypted (wrapped) form.
Key encryption key: a key used only to encrypt (wrap) other keys, such as DEKs. In a KMS it stays inside the service.
Encrypting one key with another. Unwrapping decrypts it again; re-wrapping encrypts it under a different wrapping key without touching the data.

AES in Galois/Counter Mode: authenticated encryption that both hides data and detects tampering, using a nonce and producing an authentication tag. Reusing a nonce with the same key breaks its security.
A number used once: a value that must never repeat with the same key, needed by modes like AES-GCM.
A short value produced by authenticated encryption and stored with the ciphertext; decryption fails if the data or tag was altered.
Data in readable, unencrypted form.
Amazon Elastic Block Store: network-attached disk volumes for EC2 instances.
An identity given to a running service (rather than a person), used to obtain short-lived credentials without storing long-lived keys.
Credentials that expire after minutes or hours, so a stolen copy is useful only briefly.
Granting elevated access only when requested for a specific task, time-limited and logged, instead of standing admin rights.

Server-side request forgery: tricking a server into making requests to URLs the attacker chooses, such as internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint. OWASP 2025 counts it under broken access control.
A local HTTP endpoint (169.254.169.254 on AWS) that tells a cloud instance about itself and hands out the temporary credentials of its role.
Version 2 of the AWS instance metadata service, which requires a session token obtained with a PUT request and limits network hops, blocking many simple SSRF attacks.
An IP address only valid on the local network segment (169.254.0.0/16 in IPv4). Cloud metadata services live at 169.254.169.254.
A 2019 data breach in which an attacker used an SSRF flaw in a misconfigured web application firewall to steal its AWS role credentials and read S3 data on over 100 million people.
Storing passwords, API keys and tokens in a dedicated service that authenticates who asks, authorises per secret, audits access and supports rotation, instead of in code or config files.
A widely used secrets manager that can also issue dynamic, short-lived database credentials.
Credentials created on demand for one client with a short lease and revoked automatically, so no long-lived shared password exists.
A script Git runs before accepting a commit, which can block commits containing secrets.
Google's zero-trust model for employee access, letting staff work from untrusted networks by checking user and device on every request instead of relying on a VPN.

aliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology
definition: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology, which publishes widely used security standards.
NIST's 2020 publication defining zero trust architecture.
The traditional model of a hard outer boundary (firewall, VPN) around a trusted internal network. Once inside, an attacker can often move freely.
Virtual private cloud: a logically isolated private network inside a public cloud.
A component that decides whether a request is allowed by evaluating written rules against who is asking, for what, and in what context.
The security state of a device (patched, managed, encrypted) used as part of a zero-trust access decision.
OWASP's ranked list of the most critical web application security risks, updated every few years; the lesson uses the 2025 edition.
OWASP 2025 risk A01: users can act outside their permissions, for example reading another customer's invoice. In 2025 it also covers SSRF.
OWASP 2025 risk A02: insecure settings such as default passwords, open storage or verbose errors.
OWASP 2025 risk A03: compromise through dependencies, build systems or distribution, broadening 2021's vulnerable components category.
OWASP 2025 risk A04: missing or weak encryption, poor key handling or weak algorithms that expose data.
OWASP 2025 risk A05: untrusted input interpreted as code or commands, such as SQL injection or cross-site scripting.
OWASP 2025 risk A06: flaws in the design itself that no implementation can fix, addressed by threat modelling early.

A failed or flawed authentication. A single wrong password is an ordinary authentication failure; OWASP 2025 risk A07, Authentication Failures, is the category of weak login, session or credential handling that lets attackers impersonate users.
OWASP 2025 risk A08: trusting code, updates or data without verifying they haven't been tampered with.
OWASP 2025 risk A09: missing audit logs or alerts, so attacks go unnoticed.
OWASP 2025 risk A10 (new): poor error handling such as failing open, swallowing exceptions or leaking internal details in error messages.
A database query where user input is passed as separate parameters rather than pasted into the SQL text, which prevents SQL injection.
Escaping data for the context it is placed in (HTML, URL, JavaScript) so it is shown as text and not run as code.
Systematically working out what could go wrong in a design, who might attack it and how, and which controls are needed.
Digitally signing software so consumers can verify who produced it and that it hasn't been altered.
The AWS service that records API calls made in an account, including KMS key use, for auditing.
A DDoS attack that tries to saturate network bandwidth with sheer volume, often measured in terabits per second.
A DDoS technique: the attacker sends small requests with the victim's spoofed address to open servers, which send much larger replies to the victim. The size ratio is the amplification factor.
A DDoS attack that sends many TCP connection-opening (SYN) packets without completing the handshake, filling the server's connection table.
The numbered layers of the OSI networking model; in security talk L3 is the network layer (IP), L4 transport (TCP/UDP) and L7 the application layer (HTTP).
The unit of network data rate. 1 Mbps = 1 million bits per second, 1 Gbps = 1,000 Mbps, 1 Tbps = 1,000 Gbps.
Identifying automated clients (bots) by behaviour and fingerprints; a botnet is a network of compromised machines an attacker controls.
A provider-run service (such as AWS Shield, Cloudflare or Google Cloud Armor) that absorbs and filters attack traffic across a large edge network before it reaches you.
All the points where an attacker could try to get in, such as open ports, public endpoints and admin panels.
Sending packets with a forged source IP address, which makes replies go to someone else.
An internet best practice (RFC 2827) for networks to drop outgoing packets with source addresses that don't belong to them, preventing spoofing.
The most widely used version control system. Deleting a file does not remove it from earlier commits in the history.
An identity for a program rather than a person, used to authenticate workloads.
A key-value pair recorded on a trace span, such as http.route or a customer ID. Unlike metric labels, attributes can hold high-cardinality values because each trace is stored individually.
The logarithm to base e (about 2.718): ln(x) is the power you raise e to to get x. ln(100) is about 4.6.
Estimating a value between two known points by assuming a straight line between them.
Growth by a constant factor per step, such as doubling each time, so values become very large quickly.

Bursts of retries that arrive together because many clients failed at the same moment and all wait exactly the same backoff before retrying. Each wave is a load spike that can knock the recovering service over again; adding random jitter to the waits spreads the retries out.
example: 1,000 clients that fail together and back off for exactly 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms all hit the server at the same three instants.

definition: The common short name for OpenTelemetry, the CNCF project that provides vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs and a collector for generating and exporting traces, metrics and logs.

A retry-backoff variant that waits half of the exponential-backoff delay for certain, plus a random amount up to the other half. It guarantees a minimum wait, but in Marc Brooker's AWS simulations it did more work and took longer than full jitter.
example: With a 400 ms backoff, equal jitter waits somewhere between 200 and 400 ms.

definition: A retry-backoff variant in which each wait is chosen at random between the base delay and three times the previous wait, capped at a maximum. In Marc Brooker's AWS simulations it finished slightly sooner than full jitter but made more calls.
example: After a 300 ms wait, the next wait is a random value between the 100 ms base and 900 ms.

definition: PostgreSQL's strongest table lock: it conflicts with every other lock mode, so while it is held (or waiting) even plain SELECT queries on the table are blocked. Most ALTER TABLE forms and DROP TABLE take it.
PostgreSQL's weakest table lock, taken by every SELECT that reads a table. It conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so a long-running query holding it makes a waiting ALTER TABLE queue.
A book by Michael Nygard (first edition 2007, second 2018) on designing software to survive production. It popularised stability patterns such as circuit breakers, bulkheads and timeouts.
The probability distribution of how many independent, rare events happen in a fixed interval. Its variance equals its mean, so a count of about N events typically varies by about √N.
example: If a canary expects 100 errors in ten minutes, random variation alone makes 90 or 110 unremarkable (√100 = 10).
